source_text: Here's a concrete example, a bit related to Doordash actually.  Instead of "we bring food to your house", how about simply "we bring food to your neighbourhood".  That's what corner shops do.  And yet in plenty of urban settings there are "food deserts" where people don't have access to healthy food and where people don't know where a tomato comes from or what one looks like.  So, possibly a "corner store co-op" would be in-demand in these neighbourhoods (and possibly not).

And yet in plenty of urban settings there are "food deserts" where people don't have access to healthy food and where people don't know where a tomato comes from or what one looks like.

reply_text:
㊥ (gist) This is a good test case, and there's real evidence on both sides of your "(and possibly not)". I've written it up as a worked scattering in §3.8 (`e3305d5`). The short version: supply is a tooling problem a co-op can fix, while most of the gap is demand, which is a human problem.

㊢ ("and possibly not") The evidence against:
- **Allcott, Diamond & Dubé** (NBER, later published in *QJE*) used supermarket openings and families moving between neighbourhoods. They found no meaningful effect on healthy eating. Giving low-income households the same availability and prices as high-income ones closes only **9%** of the nutrition gap; the other 91% is demand. In R-node terms the gap sits mostly in C: habits, and knowing what a tomato is.
- **Renaissance Community Co-op** in Greensboro was a community-owned grocery in a food desert. It opened in 2016 after 18 years without a store, with $1.2M raised from members plus city and county grants. It closed in 2019 because sales were too low. The post-mortem's summary: "people had developed other habits."

㊟ (but at store level) Healthy-corner-store programmes do report that when shops stock fresh produce, customers buy more of it and fewer sugary drinks. Both findings can be true: a real effect store by store can still close little of the gap across a population.

🈖 (two co-ops in one phrase) "Corner store co-op" can mean two different things:
- **A consumer co-op store** (the Renaissance model). It replaces the corner shop, so it carries every cost: capital, lease, staff, demand.
- **A purchasing co-op of existing corner stores.** It keeps the shops and their owners, the component that has lasted (NYC has 14,000+ bodegas, about 12 for every grocery store). It pools only the hard part. Distributors' minimum orders are too big for a small store, and fresh food needs refrigeration. **Saba Grocers** in Oakland does exactly this: refrigeration plus collective purchasing so shops can order below wholesale minimums. It has grown from 3 pilot stores in 2020 to 14 by July 2025.

The second version is the Arthur point from §3.6 applied: build around what has lasted.

㊭ (where the outer loop fits) The tech side is small and cheap:
- pooled ordering across stores
- item-level sales and spoilage records
- checks against SNAP/WIC stocking rules

FUTON's habit of keeping the record adds one more thing. Across stores, it would show which demand-side efforts move sales and which don't: cooking demos, tasting, the owner recommending something. That's the 91% question asked store by store, and it's where a co-op of co-ops would learn something no single shop can.

Sources:
- [NBER Digest: Eliminating food deserts won't cure nutritional inequality](https://www.nber.org/digest/feb18/eliminating-food-deserts-wont-cure-nutritional-inequality)
- [Stanford GSB working paper](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/working-papers/geography-poverty-nutrition-food-deserts-food-choices-across-united)
- [NPQ: The ballad of the RCC](https://nonprofitquarterly.org/the-ballad-of-the-rcc-or-nice-try-now-try-again/)
- [WFMY: Greensboro co-op to close](https://wfmynews2.com/article/news/greensboro-community-grocery-store-that-opened-nearly-3-years-ago-to-close/83-d6296585-6d10-4242-9c28-0b8c2d938a48)
- [UC ANR: Saba case study](https://ucanr.edu/sites/default/files/2025-09/Saba%20Case%20Study%20Brief.pdf)
- [NYU Stern FoodMapNY report](https://stern.nyu.edu/sites/default/files/2024-11/2b_FoodMapNY_ProjectReport_HealthyFoodinRetail_112224.pdf)

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: (gist) This fits what the mission has found. The human problems kept sitting where several parties' preferences meet. A co-op is an institution built for exactly that, because its members are the people on the out-channels. I've added §3.7 (`a7400af`) with six example cases. They're from memory, so an agent is now checking them against real co-ops and looking for more.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text:
("concrete examples (even if hypothetical to start with)") The six, each with the old component that won't go away and the place where tech gets in the way:
1. **Couriers own the delivery platform.** This is your DoorDash case seen from the other out-channel. CoopCycle already shares open-source dispatch software among bike-delivery co-ops.
2. **A home-care workers' co-op.** The barrier is Medicaid billing and care-plan paperwork.
3. **Small farms sharing food-safety traceability records.** The old component is a federal record-keeping rule, and no single farm can afford its own system. This one is also a small piece of your Mexico trade scale.
4. **A retiring owner sells to the staff.** The books, the valuation and the governance handover are the hard part.
5. **Gig workers pool their own earnings data** to see what the platform actually pays them.
6. **Freelancers share invoicing and social insurance.** Smart in Belgium is the known example.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: ("a solution (outer loop) in search of a problem") I think the co-op framing takes care of that worry, provided the outer loop is built from what several real inner loops need in common, not from what the stack already does. In Arthur's terms, the outer loop is a reusable assembly: member decisions, records, compliance checks and money, handled for several parties at once. Then a new co-op's activation energy goes mostly on its own problem. There are existing outer loops to learn from: Co-op Cloud (shared hosting), Start.coop, the Platform Cooperativism Consortium and Project Equity. The agent is checking what each of them actually provides and where they say tech is the barrier.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-13
previous_reply_acts.text: ("the person I was talking to") Who was it, and do you know which inner-loop problems they have in hand? A list from someone who's close to the problems would be better than my table. If you can find their organisation, I could look up what they've already published.
